asDecan.p: Every sign is split into three ten-degree slices, and each slice has its own planet and its own small card. Your Sun falls somewhere between twenty and twenty-nine degrees of Sagittarius, and in the Golden Dawn order that last slice goes to Saturn. Sagittarius is mutable fire ruled by Jupiter, the sign that wants more of everything, more road, more ideas, more meaning. Saturn has no special standing there. It's a visitor, neither helped nor held back, and it picks up some of Jupiter's colour while it stays. So the planet of limits and deadlines is at work in a sign with a big appetite, and the appetite turns into promises. The first slice is Mercury's, the Eight of Wands, quick and all over the place. The middle one is the Moon's, the Nine, and it's warier. Yours is the end of the sign, already leaning toward Capricorn, which Saturn rules. Your Sun card as a whole is Temperance, and this pip narrows it down to your ten degrees.

You're the person who ends up holding the list. On a group holiday you started out just wanting to go, and by the second day you've got the ferry times, the booking codes and everyone's passport numbers in a note on your phone. At work you offer to have a quick look at a colleague's report and end up rewriting it at eleven at night. A Sunday with nothing planned makes you slightly uneasy, so you fill it, a run, the gutters, a long call with your mum about her will. None of it feels heavy while you're doing it. Jupiter lets you see where everything's meant to end up, and Saturn makes it seem obvious that you're the one who gets it there, especially when nobody else is steering. Someone asks how your weekend was and you tell them what you got done.

You stay. A friend's divorce that drags on for two years, a parent's slow recovery after a fall, a cousin's business going under a bit at a time, and it doesn't have to be interesting for you to keep turning up. Most fire signs lose heart once things stop moving. You drive the three hours every second weekend and hardly mention it. And you keep your sense of humour while you do it, which is very Sagittarius. Jupiter still gets a say under all that Saturn. You're the one in the hospital corridor who gets a smile out of a tired nurse, or who says the slightly wrong thing at the wake and gets the whole family laughing for the first time in a week.

Your hobbies don't stay hobbies for long. You take up running for fun and within three months there's a training plan, a marathon entry and a spreadsheet, and you've stopped enjoying it. Friendships go the same way. A monthly dinner becomes something you organise, then something you feel you have to organise, and you quietly resent the friend who never once books the table. There's a tally too. Sagittarius is meant to be the easy-going sign that doesn't keep count, so you'd never own up to it. Someone thanks you for helping them move house and you say it was nothing, but you remember it, and the next time they can't make your birthday it stings a lot more than you let on.

When something goes wrong, a redundancy, a death in the family, a relationship ending, your first move is to take charge of the practical side. You ring the funeral director, sort the paperwork, tell everyone else to sit down. It looks like strength and partly it is. A week later you're still at it, except the jobs have got smaller and stranger, reorganising the linen cupboard at midnight, answering emails nobody sent you. You haven't cried yet, or you did once in the car and then got on with it. The people around you feel shut out, as if the grief belongs to you and they're only allowed to help with the catering. What actually helps is space, and that's the Sagittarius half of you asking. A long walk somewhere with a big sky, with one person who won't try to organise you and won't mind if you cry.

The people you fall for usually need something from you, a partner halfway through a career change, someone with a difficult family, a person who's clearly been let down before. It's an odd place for a Sagittarius to end up, given the sign's reputation for travelling light, but being useful is a way of being close that feels safe to you. Being looked after is harder. When your partner cooks after a bad day you hover in the kitchen and offer to wash up before you've finished eating. That's tough on someone who loves you, because it leaves them nowhere to put their care. The relationships that last are usually with people who are a bit stubborn about it, the kind who'll take the bag off your shoulder at the airport and refuse to give it back.

You're very employable, which is part of the problem. Hand you a vague project with a big aim, a festival, a new clinic, a fundraising drive, and you'll build the structure it was missing, the budget, the timeline, the roster. Managers notice that and give you the next one before the first is done. You do well in work with a long arc and a real purpose behind it, law, publishing, teaching, anything where years of steady effort add up to something you can point at. You struggle in a job where the finish line keeps moving, because you keep chasing it and never ask who moved it. I've seen a lot of late Sagittarians become the unofficial deputy of every team they're on, without the title or the pay. Ask for the title.

At twenty this slice of Sagittarius often seems older than it is. You might have been the one who worked two jobs through uni, or looked after a younger brother, or took a gap year and came home with a plan. There's still plenty of fire, but it tends to go into things you've promised. By the mid-thirties the load has usually got heavy enough to force a reckoning, a burnout, a health scare, a partner saying something blunt, and most people with this decan start dropping things, a committee here, a favour there, and find nothing falls apart. The fifties are often the best of it. The stamina is still there and so is the judgement about what's worth carrying, and plenty of people in this decan say they enjoy their work at fifty-five in a way they didn't at twenty-five.

Once a week, pick one thing on your plate that somebody else could do and give it to them. The school run, the minutes for the meeting, booking the restaurant for your sister's birthday. Tell them plainly what's needed and then leave it alone, no checking up, no quietly redoing it afterwards. If it comes back done differently from how you'd have done it, say thanks and let it stand. Keep a note of what you handed over and read the list back after a couple of months.
